Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old male with known asthma presented with 3 hours of chest tightness, mild dyspnea, wheeze, and non-productive cough following a recent cold; had been without his inhalers for ~1 week. Clinician assessed an asthma exacerbation and prescribed inhalers, a short course of oral steroids, a spacer, and provided safety-netting and rest advice.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Chest tightness for ~3 hours.
- Associated symptoms: Mild shortness of breath (not at rest), wheeze, slight non-productive cough; cough somewhat worse at night but persistent.
- Recent illness: Viral upper respiratory symptoms last week (sore throat, runny nose; now improved except for lingering cough).
- Exertional symptoms: More short of breath than usual when walking up stairs; not short of breath at rest.
- Chest pain: Denied; describes tightness rather than pain.
- Asthma history: Prior severe exacerbation in high school requiring hospital admission and intubation.
- Triggers/Contributors: Recent viral illness; ran out of inhalers about a week ago and has not used them since.
- Patient goals/concerns: Wants assurance of safety and access to inhalers; concerned about avoiding severe exacerbation/intubation.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma:
  - Background: Longstanding asthma; previously well-controlled on inhalers per patient.
  - Significant past event: Severe exacerbation in high school requiring intubation and several days of hospitalization.
- Atopy: Hay fever; dust allergy.
- Dermatologic: Eczema in childhood.
- Food allergy: Milk protein allergy in childhood (historical).

Medications:
- Home/previous:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler; dose/frequency not documented. Ran out ~1 week ago; not currently using.
  - Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler; dose/frequency not documented. Ran out ~1 week ago; not currently using.
- New/adjusted during visit:
  - Oral steroids (tablets): 2 tablets in the morning for 5 days; drug name/strength not documented.
  - Spacer device provided with instructions.
  - Refills/prescriptions issued for salbutamol (Ventolin) and beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhalers.
- Allergies:
  - Drug allergies: None reported.
  - Environmental: Dust; hay fever.

Social History:
- Was away at university last week.
- Work: Advised to rest; can self-certify off work for up to 7 days.
- Tobacco/alcohol/substances: Not documented.

Family History:
- Mother: Eczema.
- Father: Asthma.

Physical Examination:
- No vitals documented.
- No in-person physical examination performed (telemedicine consult).

Investigations:
- None performed. No peak flow available.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Asthma exacerbation likely triggered by recent viral URI and lapse in controller/reliever inhaler use.
  - Plan:
    - Prescribe/replace salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler (reliever) PRN for wheeze/shortness of breath.
    - Prescribe/replace beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler (controller); instructed to use daily (noted “in the morning” in discussion).
    - Short course of oral steroids: 2 tablets each morning for 5 days (drug/strength not documented). Side effects reviewed (possible mood changes, hyperglycemia, rash, nausea, headache); advised to read medication label.
    - Provide spacer with use instructions.
    - Safety-netting:
      - If needing salbutamol more frequently than every 3 hours, seek medical attention.
      - Seek urgent care for any deterioration: worsening shortness of breath, chest tightness/pain, light-headedness, or other concerning symptoms.
    - Rest advised; prescription to be made available within about an hour.
- Issue 2: Recent viral upper respiratory infection with improving nasal/throat symptoms; persistent cough.
  - Plan:
    - No specific additional therapy discussed; monitor as asthma management initiated.
- Issue 3: Medication supply gap/nonadherence due to running out of inhalers.
  - Plan:
    - Re-issue prescriptions and reinforce distinction between maintenance (beclomethasone) and reliever (salbutamol).
    - Provide spacer and technique reinforcement.

- General Plan items if applicable:
  - Follow up with a clinician if symptoms do not improve or if any red flags occur.
  - Time off work and rest as needed; self-certify for up to 7 days.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements:
  - Vitals, oxygen saturation, and respiratory exam findings.
  - Peak flow measurement or objective assessment of severity.
  - Detailed dosing/strength for inhalers and oral steroid name/strength.
  - Smoking, alcohol, and substance use history.
  - Comprehensive medication reconciliation beyond asthma meds.
  - Formal asthma action plan and inhaler technique check (verbal instructions provided; technique not assessed).
- Internal conflicts:
  - None significant. Patient notes overall feeling worse now vs. improved nasal symptoms; no conflict noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear; minor audio dropouts noted during steroid counseling but key information restated.
